title: Enhancing the performance and interpretability of epigenetic clocks.
data_url: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18672348 (paper's processed data, 2.4 GB) ; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE207605 (public upstream curated table used instead)

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and opened all 19 curated cohort files at GEO accession GSE207605 (32 MB gzipped, the public deposit of the upstream dataset this paper reuses): 11,910 blood samples, 0 duplicate sample IDs, age present for every sample (0 missing, range 0-103 years, mean 42.65), methylation 'beta' fractions all within 0-1, worst per-cohort missingness 0.44%. Cohorts carry different numbers of probes (934-2,374; union 2,374; 789 shared by all 19). Downloaded the paper's code release (Zenodo 20611646, 6.4 MB, GPL-3.0) and read the trained model with R: 14,006 probes grouped into 4,800 clusters, 268 clusters with non-zero weights covering 548 probes. Counted the overlap: only 466 of those 14,006 probes, 115 of the 548, and 73 of 268 weighted clusters exist in the public table. Opened the paper's Supplementary Table 1 (298 probes with target gene, correlation, weight, hg38 coordinates); 66 of 298 are in the public table. Confirmed positive-control signal directly: in cohort GSE40279 (656 samples) the classic ageing probe cg16867657 (ELOVL2 gene) correlates 0.859 with age, cg06639320 (FHL2) 0.747. Listed the paper's 2.4 GB Zenodo archive by fetching its first 2.97 MB and reading the tar index: it is a tar.gz containing Data/gaining_met.bed (1.19 MB) and Data/validation_meth.csv (831.8 MB).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: All reported accuracies (TFMethyl median absolute error 1.86 years on the 2,141-sample test split and 2.07 years on the 665-sample held-out cohort GSE84727; GP-clock 2.31; Horvath2 2.82; Horvath1 5.95; Hannum 6.29; PhenoAge 3.79; mortality hazard ratios in Generation Scotland). Also the composition of the paper's own training matrix (254,028 probes x 7,803 samples) - that file, beta_matrix.csv, is not in the data release; the repository README states it is 'available only on requests', so I never saw it.

a1_downloadable.note: Mixed, and the distinction matters. The paper's own training matrix (beta_matrix.csv) is 'available only on requests' (verified in the code README), and the Generation Scotland mortality analysis needs an access committee (~6 weeks). But the upstream curated dataset the paper reuses is fully public at GEO GSE207605: I downloaded all 19 files anonymously, no login. A1 passes only via that public substitute.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Age is literally the first row of every public cohort file ('age,90.000,90.000,...' per sample), in years, for all 11,910 samples. Nothing to construct. Verified in the files.

a3_inputs_present.note: Methylation beta values are present as numbers, probes as Illumina 450K identifiers; no lookups needed. Caveat verified: the public table carries only 2,374 probes (789 shared by all cohorts), not the 254,028 the paper used.

a4_units_stated.note: Beta value = fraction of DNA copies methylated, bounded 0-1; I confirmed every cohort's values lie in 0-1. Age in years. Both stated in the GEO series description.

a5_enough_rows.note: 11,910 labelled samples counted in the files, 0 duplicates. Caveat: 1,893 of them (cohorts GSE105018 and GSE154566, twin studies) all have age exactly 18.0, so they carry no age variation.

a6_fits_laptop.note: 32 MB gzipped on disk; the joined 11,910 x 2,374 matrix is 0.095 GB in memory. Verified by assembling it. The paper's own release is 2.4 GB and its 831 MB validation matrix exceeds the download cap, but is not needed for this route.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The public data counts exactly as GEO documents (11,910). The paper itself disagrees with itself: methods say train 4,995 / test 2,143, results say 4,997 / 2,141, and its per-cohort counts (e.g. 1,651 for GSE105018) differ from the public deposit (1,658) because it kept only probes measured in all samples. Noted, not fatal for the public route.

a8_label_provenance.note: Age is a donor record, not a model output, and is not computable from the methylation features. One real caution verified: the 2,374 probes in the public table were themselves chosen for age correlation using these same samples, so the features (not the label) were selected with knowledge of the labels.

B1.why: 19 separate cohort files, same format, concatenate on probe identifier; I did the join successfully.

B2.why: Plain gzipped CSV, parsed first try with pandas, all 19 files.

B3.why: Beta values 0-1 but normalised separately by 19 labs on two array platforms; comparable only after cohort-aware handling.

B4.why: No censored or qualitative values; worst per-cohort missingness 0.44%, verified in files.

B5.why: Counted 11,910 sample identifiers, 0 duplicates across all 19 files.

B6.why: GEO series description states beta values plus donor age; no per-column dictionary or sex/ancestry fields in the files.

C1.why: Leave-one-cohort-out decay of clock accuracy is informative whichever way it comes out.

C2.why: Saturated: GP-age, TFMethyl, AltumAge, DeepStrataAge, MethylGPT, CpGPT all open or published with honest held-out evaluation.

C3.why: Angle is 'better evaluation' across 19 cohorts, but AltumAge already published cross-dataset evaluation.

C4.why: Arrays are costly to run, but age prediction itself is solved cheaply by a penalised linear model.

C5.why: Published numbers on a named split: TFMethyl 2.07, GP-clock 2.31, Horvath2 2.82 years on GSE84727.

D1.why: MethylGPT and CpGPT are methylation backbones, but I did not verify downloadable weights or licence.

D2.why: Those backbones expect tens of thousands of probes per sample; our public table has 2,374, and CPU embedding of 11,910 samples is impractical.

D3.why: CpGPT is reported non-commercial; MethylGPT licence unchecked. Unclear rather than blocking.

E1.why: Cohort identity is the split; each cohort is its own file, verified.

E2.why: 19 cohorts, 10 of them over 300 samples, counted in the files.

E3.why: Global mean age (42.65) and per-cohort mean are directly computable; I computed the global mean.

E4.why: No replicate structure visible in the public files; age recorded to 3 decimals in some cohorts, integers in others.

E5.why: Verified: cg16867657 (ELOVL2) correlates 0.859 with age in GSE40279; present in the 789-probe common core.

E6.why: Label shuffling and per-cohort shuffling are trivial on a 0.1 GB table.

E7.why: 19 independently produced cohorts, including the GSE84727 cohort both prior papers held out.

E8.why: Verified blocker: only 115 of TFMethyl's 548 selected probes exist publicly, so its 2.07-year number cannot be reproduced.

G1.why: Illumina 450K probe identifiers plus GEO sample identifiers; hg38 coordinates in Supplementary Table 1.

G2.why: Probe identifier joins to the Illumina manifest, EWAS Atlas and ENCODE blood transcription-factor ChIP-seq, as the paper itself does.

G3.why: Probe to genomic coordinate is one-to-one; I joined 298 supplementary probes to the panel without ambiguity.

G4.why: Combined question (does binding context explain which probes drift with age) is partly answered by this paper already.

H1.why: Full outcome range present: 879 samples under 18, 2,648 aged 60+, counted in the files.

H2.why: 19 cohorts and two array platforms, but blood only and cohorts are mostly European-ancestry; no ancestry column in the files.

H3.why: The claim can be written in one precise sentence (see honest_claim_h3).

H4.why: Cohort composition is documented upstream, but the two age-18-only cohorts and ancestry skew are not flagged in the paper.

I1.why: Named users: the Hoffmann lab, the Marioni group at Edinburgh, forensic age-estimation laboratories.

I2.why: A cohort-transfer benchmark would nudge which clock people apply to a new cohort, not redirect an experiment.

I3.why: Median absolute error in years is exactly the number users of a clock quote and act on.

I4.why: A penalised linear model on 30 probes already reaches ~2 years; the mapping is close to linear, so heavy ML adds little.

J1.why: Good practice in grouped splits and controls, but the modelling itself is linear regression, not transfer learning.

J2.why: Predictions are ages in years against known ages; nonsense is immediately visible.

J3.why: A cleaned 11,910 x 789 cohort-annotated table plus a leave-one-cohort-out benchmark is shareable on its own.

J4.why: Roughly two to three weeks implied by the small data, but no budget is written down.

J5.why: No kill date or condition recorded anywhere for this candidate.

existing_models.name: TFMethyl Clock (this paper, elastic net on 4,800 median-aggregated probe clusters)
existing_models.score_and_split: Median absolute error 1.86 years on a 2,141-sample random test split and 2.07 years (correlation 0.97) on the held-out cohort GSE84727 (665 samples), from the paper text
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Why most clock probes sit outside transcription-factor binding sites, and that errors still rise sharply in samples over 60 for every clock tested

existing_models.name: GP-age (Gaussian process regression on 30 probes, Varshavsky et al. 2023)
existing_models.score_and_split: Median error ~2.1 years on held-out blood data in its own paper; 2.31 years on GSE84727 as re-measured by this paper
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Extending beyond fixed-rate linear methylation change and transferring array-trained models to sequencing data

existing_models.name: AltumAge (deep neural network on 20,318 probes, pan-tissue)
existing_models.score_and_split: Mean absolute error 2.302 years versus 2.621 for an elastic net, evaluated both within and across datasets
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Generalisation to older ages and to tissue types absent from training; could not compare with DeepMAge because that code is unavailable

existing_models.name: DeepStrataAge (2026 deep clock, 12,234 probes, 29,167 training samples)
existing_models.score_and_split: 1.89 years mean absolute error on a separate validation cohort, reported to beat published deep and elastic-net clocks

existing_models.name: MethylGPT / CpGPT (transformer foundation models for DNA methylation)
existing_models.score_and_split: MethylGPT pretrained on 226,555 profiles (154,063 after quality control) from 5,281 datasets; both report state-of-the-art age prediction after fine-tuning
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Imputing genome-wide methylation from sparse input and linking representations to disease risk

backbone.name: MethylGPT / CpGPT (methylation transformers); no protein or DNA backbone applies
backbone.hardware: GPU expected; the public 2,374-probe panel is far thinner than the ~49,000-probe vocabulary these models expect
backbone.licence: Not verified; CpGPT is reported non-commercial

integration.partner_dataset: ENCODE blood transcription-factor ChIP-seq peaks and the JASPAR motif set, joined via the Illumina 450K manifest's hg38 coordinates (the paper's own Data/CpGs_to_TFBS.bed does exactly this)
integration.join_key: Illumina 450K probe identifier -> hg38 genomic coordinate
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does the regulatory context of a CpG site predict whether its methylation drifts with age, independently of the person-level clock?

controls.positive_control: cg16867657 in the ELOVL2 gene must come out as a top age-associated probe; verified it correlates 0.859 with age in GSE40279 and sits in the 789-probe core shared by all cohorts
controls.negative_control: Shuffle ages within each cohort and confirm error collapses to the per-cohort mean baseline; also train on the two age-18-only cohorts to confirm the model cannot learn from zero-variance labels
controls.external_validation: Hold out whole cohorts (GSE84727 reproduces the split both prior papers used), and compare array-trained predictions against the independent cohorts GSE40279 and GSE157131

honest_claim_h3: On publicly deposited blood methylation from 11,910 donors, restricted to 2,374 probes that were themselves pre-selected for age correlation on these same donors, we can say how much a clock's accuracy degrades when it is tested on a cohort it never saw - but not whether transcription-factor-binding features help, because 79% of the probes this paper's model uses are absent from the public data.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use blood DNA methylation levels at selected sites to predict a person's age, and measure how accuracy drops on unseen cohorts.
plain_idea.train_on: Methylation fraction (0-1) at up to 2,374 sites per blood sample, for 11,910 samples from 19 studies; I verified this count and that every sample has an age.
plain_idea.predict: The donor's chronological age in years. The true answer comes from the donor record attached to each sample in the original study, not from any model.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Clock users (forensic laboratories, ageing cohorts) quote one error figure, usually from a single held-out cohort; knowing how that figure decays across 19 independent cohorts would tell them what to expect on their own samples.

more_or_better_data.why: Our usable public table is 11,910 samples and 2,374 probes; MethylGPT was pretrained on 226,555 profiles and DeepStrataAge trained on 29,167 samples with 12,234 probes. Even this paper's own model used 254,028 probes, which we cannot get.

confidence_score.why: No replicate measurements are visible in the public files, and age is recorded at mixed precision (integers in some cohorts, three decimals in others), so a calibrated per-sample uncertainty cannot be grounded; GP-age already outputs a Gaussian-process variance.

models_beatable.why: TFMethyl (2026) and GP-age (2023) are both already evaluated on a genuinely held-out cohort, and DeepStrataAge reports 1.89 years on a separate cohort; there is no weak random-split number left to pick off.

guaranteed_improvement.why: The first condition fails outright: TFMethyl cannot be run as our baseline, because only 115 of its 548 selected probes and 73 of its 268 weighted clusters exist in the public data, which I checked directly.

ml_idea: Project considered and declined: assemble the public 11,910-sample, 19-cohort blood methylation table (GEO GSE207605) and run a leave-one-cohort-out benchmark of age prediction, testing whether this paper's two ideas - restricting features to transcription-factor binding sites and median-aggregating correlated probes into clusters - survive out-of-cohort evaluation. It dies on two verified facts: the probe panel is too thin to carry the paper's features (466 of 14,006), and the panel was selected for age correlation on the very samples we would evaluate on.

effort.compute_note: Measured, not guessed: I downloaded the 32 MB of cohort files and assembled the 11,910 x 2,374 table in well under an hour; the joined matrix is 0.095 GB as 64-bit floats. The 15 minutes for one 19-fold leave-one-cohort-out elastic-net run is an estimate from that matrix size, not timed.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count how many of the published model's selected probes exist in the public data. I ran it: 115 of 548 probes and 73 of 268 weighted clusters, so the published model cannot be run as a baseline on anything downloadable.

verdict_reason: Part A passes, but only through a substitute dataset, and the project behind it is already served. The paper's own training matrix (254,028 probes x 7,803 samples) is 'available only on requests' and its Generation Scotland analysis needs an access committee; the public upstream deposit I did open (11,910 samples, age for all, 0 duplicates, 0.1 GB) carries just 2,374 probes, of which only 466 overlap the paper's 14,006 features and only 115 of its 548 selected ones - so the published 2.07-year result cannot be reproduced or beaten on open data. Meanwhile the task is the most crowded in computational epigenetics (GP-age, AltumAge, DeepStrataAge, MethylGPT, CpGPT, all with honest held-out numbers around 1.9-2.3 years), a penalised linear model already reaches that, and no pretrained backbone fits a 2,374-probe panel. Worse, those probes were chosen for age correlation using these same samples, so even the one honest angle - a leave-one-cohort-out re-evaluation - starts contaminated.
